title: A fair price for a bet
objectives: Price a bet by its expected value.
Compute a bet's expected profit and say who it favours
Recognise a fair bet as one with zero expected profit

screens.title: Is £2 a good price?
screens.prose: I offer you a ticket for £2. It pays £10 if two dice total 7, and nothing otherwise. The grid shows every total.
screens.question: Should you buy it?

options.text: No: on average a ticket returns less than £2
Yes: 7 is the most likely total
options.why: You priced the ticket by the most likely total. Even 7 comes up only one roll in six, and every other roll pays nothing.

options.text: Yes: a win pays five times the price
options.why: You priced it by the winning case alone. Five times the price is not enough when you win only one time in six.

options.text: You cannot tell before the dice are rolled
options.why: One roll is unpredictable, but the average over many tickets is not. That average decides whether a price is good.

hints.text: How often does a total of 7 come up?
Six of the 36 cells total 7.
One ticket in six pays £10. So on average a ticket returns £10 ÷ 6.

feedback.correct: A ticket returns about £1.67 on average, less than the £2 it costs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about many tickets: how many pay, and how much do they pay back in total?

byKey.likely: You priced the ticket by the most likely total. Five tickets in six still pay nothing.

explain.text: Six of the 36 outcomes total 7, so one ticket in six pays £10. Over many tickets you get back about £10 ÷ 6 ≈ £1.67 each. Paying £2 loses about 33p a ticket on average.

screens.title: Find the break-even price
screens.prose: Now set the price yourself. Run tickets and watch your average profit per ticket. Then slide the price until that profit is close to zero.

derive.caption: {{ran ? 'Price ' + money(price) + '. Average profit per ticket over ' + ran + ' tickets: ' + money(10 * values['1'] / ran - price) : 'Price ' + money(price) + '. Run some tickets.'}}

screens.question: Run 1,000 tickets. At about what price is your average profit per ticket zero?

options.text: About £1.67
About £5
options.why: You halved the £10, as if a 7 came up half the time. It comes up about one time in six.
That is what a winning ticket pays. You win only about one ticket in six.

options.text: About £0.28
options.why: You used 1/36, the chance of one cell. Six cells total 7.

hints.text: Run 1,000 tickets first, then move the price.
The average profit is the average payout minus the price. Slide the price until the caption reads close to £0.00.

feedback.correct: About one ticket in six pays £10, so the average payout is about £1.67.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run 1,000 tickets and slide the price until the caption is close to zero.

explain.text: Over 1,000 tickets about one in six paid £10, so a ticket returned about £1.67 on average. At that price your average profit is close to zero. Above it you lose in the long run, and below it you gain.

screens.title: The fair price
screens.prose: The price at which the average profit is zero is the bet's **fair price**. It is the expected payoff: $E[\text{payoff}] = 10 \cdot P(\text{total} = 7)$.
screens.question: What is the fair price of the ticket, in pounds?

widget.label: Fair price
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{10}{6}$, such as 1.67

hints.text: Six of the 36 cells pay £10. The rest pay £0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each payoff by its chance and add.

byKey.cell: You used the chance of one cell, 1/36. Six cells total 7.
byKey.half: You treated winning and losing as equally likely. A ticket wins one time in six.
byKey.payout: That is the payoff when it pays. Five tickets in six pay nothing.

explain.text: $E[\text{payoff}] = 10 \cdot \tfrac{6}{36} + 0 \cdot \tfrac{30}{36} = \tfrac{10}{6} \approx 1.67$. The losing outcomes add nothing to the sum. They still matter: they are why the winning chance is only $\tfrac{1}{6}$.

screens.title: Expected profit
screens.prose: You buy the ticket at £2. Your profit on a ticket is its payoff minus the £2 you paid.
screens.question: What is your expected profit per ticket, in pounds?

widget.placeholder: a negative number means a loss
widget.label: Expected profit
widget.accept: any form equal to $-\tfrac{1}{3}$, such as −0.33

hints.text: Your average payoff is £1.67. What did you pay?
Expected profit $= 1.67 - 2$.

feedback.correct: You lose about 33p a ticket on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the price away from the expected payoff.

byKey.sign: You subtracted the wrong way round. You pay £2 and get back £1.67 on average, so you are down.
byKey.win: That is your profit when you win. Five tickets in six lose the £2.
byKey.price: You left out the payoff. A ticket returns £1.67 on average, not nothing.

explain.text: Expected profit $= E[\text{payoff}] - \text{price} = 1.67 - 2 = -0.33$. A bet favours the buyer only when the price is below $E[\text{payoff}]$. At £2 this one favours the seller.

screens.title: Two ways to win
screens.prose: A new ticket pays £12 if the total is 7, and £6 if the total is 2 or 12. Anything else pays nothing.
screens.question: What is the fair price of this ticket, in pounds?

widget.label: Fair price
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{7}{3}$, such as 2.33

hints.text: Two payoffs, each with its own chance.
Two cells pay £6.
$12 \cdot \tfrac{6}{36} + 6 \cdot \tfrac{2}{36}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh each payoff by its own chance, then add.

byKey.sum: You added the two payoffs. No roll pays both, and each pays only with its own chance.
byKey.first: You priced only the 7. The totals 2 and 12 add another 33p.
byKey.plain: You averaged £12 and £6 as if one of them always paid. Most rolls pay nothing.
byKey.one-end: You counted only one of the two cells that pay £6. Both (1, 1) and (6, 6) do.

explain.text: $12 \cdot \tfrac{6}{36} + 6 \cdot \tfrac{2}{36} = \tfrac{72 + 12}{36} = \tfrac{7}{3} \approx 2.33$. Each payoff is weighted by its own chance. A price of £2.33 is fair.

screens.title: A fair coin bet
screens.prose: You pay £1. A fair coin is tossed. Heads pays you £2, and tails pays nothing.
screens.question: Is this a good bet for you?

options.text: It is fair: the expected profit is £0
It is good: half the time you double your money
options.why: You looked only at heads. Tails loses your £1 just as often.

options.text: It is bad: half the time you lose your £1
options.why: You looked only at tails. Heads gains £1 just as often.

hints.text: Find the expected payoff first.
Expected payoff $= 2 \times 0.5 = 1$. Compare it with the £1 price.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the expected payoff with the price.

byKey.good: You called a zero-profit bet good. It has no edge in your favour, only risk.

explain.text: The expected payoff is $2 \times 0.5 = 1$, exactly the price, so the expected profit is 0. A fair bet is not a good bet: it has no edge, only risk. Casinos and market makers live on bets priced a little away from fair.

screens.title: Rare but large
screens.prose: A contract pays £100 if a stock crashes this month, and £0 otherwise. The chance of a crash is 0.05.
screens.question: What is the contract's fair price?

options.why: You priced it by the most likely outcome. It usually pays nothing, but the rare £100 is worth something in advance.
You priced it by the payoff in the case that pays. That happens only one month in twenty.
You averaged £0 and £100 as if equally likely. A crash has chance 0.05, not 0.5.

hints.text: Weigh each payoff by its chance.
The crash bar is short, but its payoff is large.

feedback.correct: £100 one month in twenty is worth £5 a month.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each payoff by its chance and add.

byKey.zero: You priced it by its most likely outcome, £0. A fair price weighs every outcome by its chance.

explain.text: $E[\text{payoff}] = 100 \times 0.05 + 0 \times 0.95 = 5$. Pricing by the most likely outcome gives £0. Pricing by the payoff when it pays gives £100, and both ignore part of the pmf.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: Every price you set followed one rule. The fair price of a bet is its expected payoff. Then $$E[\text{profit}] = E[\text{payoff}] - \text{price}.$$ The buyer is favoured when the price is below $E[\text{payoff}]$.
screens.question: A bet has $E[\text{payoff}] = \text{£}4$ and costs £4.50. Which is true?

options.text: Expected profit is −£0.50, so it favours the seller
Expected profit is +£0.50, so it favours the buyer
options.why: You subtracted the wrong way round. The price is above the expected payoff.

options.text: It is fair, since £4 and £4.50 are close
options.why: Close is not equal. The buyer loses 50p a bet on average, and that adds up.

hints.text: Expected profit is expected payoff minus price.

feedback.correct: The buyer expects to lose 50p a bet.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the price from the expected payoff.

explain.text: $E[\text{profit}] = 4 - 4.50 = -0.50$. Over 100 such bets the buyer expects to lose about £50. The seller expects to make it.

screens.title: Why the price comes straight off
screens.prose: Why is expected profit just expected payoff minus the price? Let the payoff $X$ have pmf $P(X = x)$, and let the price be $c$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $E[X - c] = \sum_x (x - c)\,P(X = x)$, since the profit is $x - c$ when the payoff is $x$
$= \sum_x x\,P(X = x) - c \sum_x P(X = x)$, splitting the sum and taking out the constant $c$
$= E[X] - c \cdot 1$, since the first sum is $E[X]$ and the chances add to 1

hints.text: Start by writing the profit for one value of the payoff.
The second line splits one sum into two.
Write the sum, split it, then use the fact that the chances add to 1.

feedback.correct: The constant comes out of the sum, and the chances add to 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the definition, then split the sum.

byKey.s2: Splitting the sum needs the sum written out first. Start with the definition.
byKey.s3: You need the split sum before you can name each part.

explain.text: The constant $c$ comes out of the sum, and the chances add to 1. So paying $c$ lowers the expected value by exactly $c$. A later lesson extends this to $E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b$.

screens.title: A binary option
screens.prose: A stock is at £100. Each day it rises £2 with chance 0.4, stays flat with chance 0.4, or falls £2 with chance 0.2. A binary option pays £100 if the price after two days is above £102.
screens.question: What is the option's fair price, in pounds?

hints.text: Which final prices are above £102?
Only one path ends above £102.
Up then up ends at £104, with chance $0.4 \times 0.4 = 0.16$. The option is worth $100 \times 0.16$.

feedback.correct: Only up, up pays: chance 0.16, so £16.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance of ending above £102, then multiply by £100.

byKey.at-102: You counted a finish at exactly £102. The option needs the price above £102, so only £104 pays.
byKey.only-102: You took the paths that end at £102. They do not pay; only up, up reaches £104.
byKey.payout: That is the payoff when it pays. It pays only when both days rise.
byKey.one-up: You needed only one rise. A rise and a flat day end at £102, which is not above £102.

explain.text: Only up, up ends above £102, with chance $0.4 \times 0.4 = 0.16$. So the fair price is $100 \times 0.16 = 16$. Option desks also price by expectation, but under probabilities read off market prices, called risk-neutral probabilities.

screens.title: The bookmaker's edge
screens.prose: A bookmaker sells £1 tickets on a football match. A ticket pays £1 if its result happens. Exactly one result will happen.

state.caption: Each ticket pays £1 if its result happens

screens.question: You buy one ticket on each result. What is your sure loss, in pounds?

hints.text: Add up what the three tickets cost.
Exactly one ticket pays out.
You pay $0.52 + 0.28 + 0.27$ and collect £1.

feedback.correct: You pay £1.07 and collect £1, whatever happens.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the total cost with the £1 you are sure to collect.

byKey.total: That is what you pay. You also collect £1 from the winning ticket.
byKey.zero: You assumed the prices are fair. They add to more than £1.

explain.text: You pay $0.52 + 0.28 + 0.27 = 1.07$ and collect exactly £1, so you lose 7p for sure. Fair prices are chances, so they would add to exactly 1. The extra 7p is the bookmaker's **overround**, its edge on every match.

ideas: A bet's fair price is its expected payoff: the price at which the average profit is zero.
Expected profit is the expected payoff minus the price. The buyer is favoured only when the price is below the expected payoff.
A fair bet has zero expected profit. That makes it fair, not good: it has no edge, only risk.

formula.name: Expected profit
formula.note: The fair price makes this zero.

summary.trap: Pricing a bet by its most likely outcome, or by its payoff when it pays. Weigh every outcome by its chance.

quiz.prose: A £2 lottery ticket wins £1,000,000 with chance 1 in 1,000,000, and £50 with chance 1 in 100. Otherwise it pays nothing.
quiz.question: What is your expected profit per ticket, in pounds?

widget.placeholder: a negative number means a loss
widget.label: Expected profit

feedback.correct: The ticket returns £1.50 on average and costs £2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the expected payoff, then take off the price.

byKey.payoff: That is the expected payoff. Take off the £2 price.
byKey.sign: You subtracted the wrong way round. The price is above the expected payoff.
byKey.jackpot: You left out the £50 prize. It adds 50p to the expected payoff.

explain.text: $E[\text{payoff}] = 1{,}000{,}000 \times 10^{-6} + 50 \times 0.01 = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5$. So the expected profit is $1.5 - 2 = -0.5$, a 50p loss per ticket.

quiz.prose: A ticket costs £3 and pays £20 if two dice show a double six.
quiz.question: What is your expected profit per ticket, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A double six has chance 1/36.

byKey.payoff: That is the expected payoff. Take off the £3 price.
byKey.win: That is your profit when you win, which happens once in 36 tickets.

explain.text: $E[\text{payoff}] = 20 \cdot \tfrac{1}{36} \approx 0.56$, so the expected profit is about $0.56 - 3 = -2.44$.

quiz.prose: Bet A costs £2 and pays £9 with chance 0.2. Bet B costs £0.90 and pays £1 with chance 0.95. Otherwise each pays nothing.
quiz.question: Which bet is favourable to the buyer?

options.text: Only B
Only A
options.why: You were drawn by the bigger payoff. A's expected payoff is $9 \times 0.2 = 1.80$, below its £2 price.

options.text: Both
options.why: A's expected payoff, £1.80, is below its £2 price.

options.text: Neither
options.why: B's expected payoff is $1 \times 0.95 = 0.95$, above its 90p price.

feedback.correct: B returns 95p on average for a 90p price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each bet's expected payoff with its price.

explain.text: A: $E = 9 \times 0.2 = 1.80 < 2$, unfavourable. B: $E = 1 \times 0.95 = 0.95 > 0.90$, favourable. The size of the prize does not decide; the expected payoff against the price does.

quiz.prose: A bet's expected profit is exactly £0.
quiz.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: It is fair: over many bets you expect to roughly break even
It is a good bet, because you cannot lose on average
options.why: Zero expected profit is no edge at all. You take risk and expect nothing for it.

options.text: You break even on every single bet
options.why: Expected profit is an average over many bets. Each bet still wins or loses.

feedback.correct: A fair bet has no edge either way.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expected profit describes the average over many bets.

explain.text: Zero expected profit means the price equals the expected payoff. Single bets still win or lose; only the long-run average is zero. That makes the bet fair, not good.
